prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, trapping atoms at a magic wavelength to reach unprecedented accuracy and stability in the measurement of time

statement.case_for: I now put optical lattice clocks first, ahead of my own opening first choice. Seven of eight members ranked it, four placed it first, and the supporting arguments are independent of one another and of field loyalty. The magic-wavelength idea (Katori) removes Doppler, recoil and light-shift limitations at once, and the realisation (Katori, then Ye's group with record systematics and the many-body Fermi-degenerate clock) brought fractional uncertainty to about 1e-18. That is a new regime: relativistic redshifts resolved across millimetres, tests of constancy of constants, and a credible path to redefining the second. It has been reproduced in Sr and Yb clocks at JILA, RIKEN, NIST, PTB, SYRTE and elsewhere, and cross-continent comparisons agree. The two-name credit is clean and matches what every member who proposed laureates wrote. As a theorist embedded in experimental teams, I value that this is a demonstration whose control of every physical detail is exceptional, and the discovery (not the application) is what is rewarded.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is distinctness from earlier recognition: the 2005 prize (Hall and Haensch, frequency combs) and the 2012 prize (Wineland and Haroche, control of single quantum systems and ion clocks) supply the comb and the quantum-control background, so a sceptic can read lattice clocks as the next increment in precision spectroscopy. Lemonde and others who contributed to the lattice-clock lineage are outside the credited set, Ye's name recurs in other candidacies, and the redefinition of the second has not yet happened, so the full payoff is still ahead. Finally, there is a framing risk that the prize rewards a measurement technology rather than a basic discovery.

responses.point: Kroll ranks lattice clocks first as a new measurement technique with 1e-18 uncertainty, and ranks circuit QED second, preferring an experiment-weighted trio (Wallraff, Schoelkopf, Girvin) and worrying about overlap with the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I agree on the clock and on the clean Katori-Ye attribution, and I take your point that early priority beyond the two names (Lemonde and others) cannot be fixed by us. On circuit QED I accept your experiment-weighted allocation as at least as defensible as mine: the strong-coupling experiment and dispersive readout are the decisive observations, and I should not have placed Blais over Girvin so confidently. I also share your caution on 2025. The 2025 citation was about macroscopic quantum tunnelling and energy quantisation in a circuit; circuit QED is a different physical idea (single-photon strong coupling), but the committee would be asked to explain that distinction publicly, and in the same decade it is a real cost. That is why I now put it as an alternative rather than first.

responses.point: Eriksson ranks magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene first for the quantitative theory prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald) followed by the 2018 experimental discovery, and ranks topological insulators and DMFT next.
responses.response: I find the theory-then-experiment link in B010 persuasive and it is the strongest condensed-matter case on the list. My reservations are about maturity and attribution, not significance: the superconducting pairing mechanism is still unsettled, device-to-device variability remains, and Yuan Cao's role in the 2018 experiments sits outside the credited trio. Compared with lattice clocks, where independent laboratories agree at the 1e-18 level, B010 is still moving. I defer to you and Olsson on the condensed-matter details, and I keep it as my second alternative rather than dismissing it.

responses.point: Pearce places lattice clocks first as a clean instrument advance that opened a new measurement regime, and ranks IceCube second as a new observational window, while flagging whether the committee wants metrology prizes close to atom interferometry.
responses.response: I agree with your reading of clocks, and your point about proximity to atom interferometry (B036) is fair: those two share laser-cooling heritage and would be a poor pairing in the same year, so I would not build a two-part prize from them. On IceCube I defer to you and Danielsson on astroparticle details, but note that your own reservation, that the origin of the bulk diffuse flux is unresolved, is the kind of maturity concern I would weigh against it this year.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks clocks first as precision-meets-theory atomic physics, and notes that Hall and Haensch's 2005 prize and Wineland's 2012 prize might make clocks look like a continuation.
responses.response: This is the most serious objection to my own preferred choice and I do not think it is empty. My answer is that the earlier prizes honoured the tools (the comb, and ion trapping and control), whereas the lattice clock introduced a new idea (magic-wavelength trapping that makes thousands of atoms interrogable without perturbing the transition) with a quantitatively new outcome. A citation that explicitly names the magic wavelength keeps the new content visible. I would value your view on whether Lemonde's contribution forces a different wording.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards lattice clocks as sufficiently distinct from the 2005 and 2012 precision-spectroscopy prizes.
Whether the credit for the magic-wavelength proposal and early lattice-clock realisations is fully captured by Katori and Ye, given Lemonde and others.
Whether circuit QED (B034) is too close to the 2025 prize, and whether Girvin or Blais belongs in the trio if it advances.
Whether twisted bilayer graphene (B010) will be judged mature enough given the unresolved pairing mechanism and the omission of Yuan Cao.
statement.conflict_note: Possible conflict on B034 (circuit QED) and B043 (optomechanics): I direct the Wallenberg Centre for Quantum Technology, work in superconducting circuits, and have close ties to groups in this field; Chalmers has hosted 2025 laureates as guest researchers. I would step back from advocating for B034 and B043 and would recuse on them if the committee requires. No specific conflict is apparent with B004 (optical lattice clocks) or the other shortlisted candidates from the provided profile.
